newsitem.title: RUSSIA: IMF boss says reform could make Russia a superpower.
newsitem.headline: IMF boss says reform could make Russia a superpower.

text.p: The head of the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday that Russia could become an economic superpower, but told the conservative parliament it would have to promote economic reform to make this possible.
"This country can be an economic superpower, but this cannot be achieved without reforms," Camdessus told the budget committee of the State Duma lower house of parliament.
"We believe this is a window of opportunity, but the State Duma has an enormous responsibility to create the necessary structure," he said.

Camdessus said annual growth could be over five percent by the turn of the century and added that he was ready to recommend that the IMF resume its lending programme to Russia after several months of delays due to doubts about low tax revenues.

"I am now ready to ask the board of directors to continue payments on the second tranche of the three-year programme," Camdessus said. "The programme for 1997-98 is almost ready and payments on the second tranche could start next month."
But Camdessus, in Moscow for talks with President Boris Yeltsin and other senior officials, said many decisions were up to the Duma, which is dominated by communists and their allies.
The Duma has not yet approved a series of documents from the government, including a tax code which ministers say is needed to underpin future spending and revenue plans.
Many top reformers in the government hold little hope the code will be passed by the Duma this year.
Deputies criticised IMF complaints about Russian natural monopolies and said it would be hard to avoid popular unrest. Millions of Russians have not received their wages and pensions on time.
"We told Camdessus that we find it increasingly difficult to restrain people's emotions," former Soviet prime minister Nikolai Ryzhkov told reporters after Camdessus met the Duma committee.

"When do you expect the fall to end?" asked Agrarian Party deputy Gennady Kulik, who accused Camdessus of standing in the way of amendments to the reform process that some Duma deputies hope will bring the Russian economy back to growth.
Yeltsin's reaction was much more positive.
"Each time you come to Russia you make a contribution to the transformation of our country," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as telling Camdessus at the start of their meeting.
"You, personally, and the experts who visit Russia on your instructions, have saved us from making many mistakes in carrying out our reforms."

The IMF, which has already allocated a total of $21 billion to back economic reforms, has urged Russia to reform its massive, monolithic natural monopolies and improve supervision of the banking system.
"We have risked $21 billion in this country to make sure this economy restarts," Camdessus said.
"I'm used to being the scapegoat for everything which does not go well in the 60 countries where we work around the world."
He said a document being prepared by Russia and the IMF would aim to strengthen central bank control over commercial banks and develop a commercial bank-funded deposit insurance scheme.
Russia needed powers to punish those who did not pay their tax and to modernise the tax service, he added.
